how-do-i-track-vendor-policy-changes.htm.text:
← Vendor change evidence

How do I track when a vendor changes its subprocessors or privacy policy?

A vendor adds a subprocessor. The page updates. No email arrives, or one arrives in a monthly digest nobody opens. Nine months later an auditor asks how you review changes to your processors, and the honest answer is that you look when you remember to.

The control that closes this is unglamorous: dated snapshots, compared on a cadence, kept as a record.

Open the free vendor change comparison

What to snapshot

  • Subprocessor list. The one with a contractual clock attached — new entries can mean new companies or new countries handling personal data.
  • Privacy notice. Changes to purposes, retention, or international transfers.
  • Terms of service or DPA. Liability, termination, and data-return language.
  • Security or trust page. Certifications that lapse quietly, and claims that quietly soften.

Why the vendor's own notification is not the control

Notification depends on the vendor's list being current, on the address they hold, and on the mail arriving somewhere a person reads. All three fail routinely, and none of them fail loudly. A snapshot you took is a fact you hold; a notification you did not receive is indistinguishable from nothing having changed.

Inconclusive is a result

The failure mode that makes a monitoring control worse than none is a clean "no changes" produced by a fetch that never happened. When a snapshot records a non-ok status — timeout, blocked, or anything else — the comparison reports inconclusive rather than stable, and says which side failed. A gap you can see is recoverable; a gap that reads as reassurance is not.

How to use it

  1. Capture snapshots of the pages you monitor, with dates and a fetch status, on whatever cadence your agreements imply.
  2. Run the comparison over the previous and current snapshot. It runs locally and never contacts the vendor or uploads anything.
  3. Export the Markdown or JSON report and file it with the date you reviewed it.
  4. Read the diff yourself. The report is evidence of what differs, not a judgement about what it means.

The tool reports evidence only. It does not decide whether a contract, a security posture, or a compliance status has changed — those are legal and commercial questions about your agreement.

Common questions

How do I track when a vendor changes its privacy policy or subprocessor list?

Capture a dated snapshot of the pages you care about — privacy notice, terms, subprocessor list, security page — on a regular cadence, then compare each new snapshot against the previous one and keep the resulting diff as your review record. What matters for an audit is not only that you noticed a change but that you can show the two versions, the dates, and the date you reviewed it. Relying on the vendor's own notification is not a control, because notification is exactly what tends to fail.

Why is a subprocessor list worth monitoring specifically?

Data processing agreements commonly give the customer a right to be informed of new subprocessors, and sometimes a window to object, because a new subprocessor can mean personal data reaching a new company or a new country. That right is only usable if you notice in time. A page that gains a line without an announcement is the ordinary case, so a dated diff is the practical way to keep the clock meaningful.

What happens if a snapshot could not be captured?

The report is inconclusive rather than stable. A snapshot that timed out, was blocked, or failed for any other reason is recorded with its non-ok status and the comparison says so explicitly. This matters because the dangerous failure mode for a monitoring control is a clean 'no changes' produced by a fetch that never happened.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, privacy, security, or compliance advice, and it does not determine whether a vendor change affects your obligations, your agreement, or your regulatory position. It compares snapshots you supply and reports differences. Whether a difference matters, and what you must do about it, depends on your contract and applicable law — take advice from a qualified professional. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage arising from its use.

Vendor Change Evidence

If a vendor changes its privacy, terms, subprocessors, or security page, paste a dated before and after snapshot and get a portable review record — entirely in your browser.

Paste your two snapshots as JSON (url, captured_at, fetch_status, text):

Don't have snapshots handy? — a small before/after pair with a real content change, so you can see the report shape before using your own.

What this is and isn't

  • Everything runs in your browser. The snapshots you paste are never uploaded — there is no server here to send them to.
  • This tool never contacts a vendor. You (or your own capture process) supply both dated snapshots; this only compares them.
  • It reports observations only — changed, unchanged, or inconclusive — and does not decide whether a contract, security posture, or compliance status changed. That judgment is yours.
  • Use fetch_status values other than "ok" (for example "timeout" or "blocked") when a capture failed. The report is marked inconclusive, never falsely stable.
  • Only anonymous, aggregate usage counts (for example "a comparison was run") may be recorded locally — never snapshot text or URLs.

Common questions

Does this fetch the vendor's page for me?

No. This tool never makes a network request to a vendor. You supply both snapshots — however you captured them — and this only compares the two. That keeps it usable for internal, access-controlled, or authenticated pages a public fetcher could never reach.

What counts as a valid snapshot?

A JSON object with four string fields: url (the page you captured), captured_at (an ISO 8601 timestamp), fetch_status ("ok" if the capture succeeded, anything else if it didn't), and text (the page content or a normalized extract of it).

Why "inconclusive" instead of "unchanged"?

If either capture failed (a non-"ok" fetch status) or the "after" timestamp is earlier than "before", the tool cannot honestly claim the page is stable — a failed fetch could be hiding a real change. It reports inconclusive rather than a false negative.

Is my snapshot text uploaded anywhere?

No. Comparison happens with JavaScript running in your own browser tab. This page makes no network request with your pasted content — there is nothing to intercept because nothing is sent. Only anonymous, aggregate usage counts like "a comparison was run" may be recorded locally, with an opt-out below.

Is there a command-line version?

Yes — the same comparison logic ships as a local Python CLI (src/vendor_change.py) in this tool's repository, for scripted or scheduled use. See the README for its usage.

How do I track when a vendor changes its subprocessors or privacy policy?

Already run a continuous vendor-risk platform? See how this tool compares to UpGuard.

Just planning to reload the page and compare it by eye? See what eyeballing two page loads actually misses.

Need to capture a vendor page now and diff it when you come back? The vendor change watch tool stores pasted captures in this browser and reports a section-by-section diff on the next paste — nothing uploaded.

vs-eyeballing-two-page-loads-side-by-sid.text:
← Vendor Change Evidence

This tool vs. eyeballing two page loads side by side

Ten words added to a page of hundreds reads naturally either way. A glance cannot tell that anything moved; a byte-for-byte diff cannot miss it.

What eyeballing two page loads tells you

Opening a vendor's privacy or subprocessor page again and comparing it to what you remember, or to a saved copy, is the cheapest, most common way anyone re-reviews a vendor page, and it is not wrong to do it: a whole new section, a moved heading, or an obviously rewritten paragraph is exactly the kind of change a person scanning for something different will catch.

What a glance is unreliable for is the change that matters most in practice: a clause added or removed inside a paragraph that still reads naturally, in a page of hundreds of words where nothing about the page's shape signals that anything moved. Nobody scanning a long policy page is running a word-by-word count against last month's version in their head.

A real pair, from this tool's own shipped example

This is not a hypothetical. It is the before/after snapshot pair shipped with this tool's own examples, reproduced exactly: 

before.json (captured 2026-08-23T09:00:00Z):
  "We process account data to provide the service."

after.json  (captured 2026-08-24T09:00:00Z):
  "We process account and usage data to provide the service."

A day apart, the same URL, the same fetch status. On a real vendor page this sentence would sit inside a much longer document, and "account data" quietly becoming "account and usage data" changes what the vendor says it collects without changing the shape of the page at all -- no new heading, no bold notice, nothing to catch the eye of someone comparing the two by scrolling and scanning.

Running this tool against the same pair instead: 

{
  "status": "changed",
  "changes": [
    { "kind": "content_changed", "before_length": 47, "after_length": 57 }
  ],
  "review_required": true,
  "evidence_boundary": "Reports observations; the customer decides
    contractual or security significance."
}

The tool does not know or care whether ten extra characters matter -- that judgment is explicitly left to you, per its own evidence_boundary. What it does not do is fail to notice the ten characters, because it never reads for meaning; it compares every character in before.text against every character in after.text.

Side by side

Eyeballing two page loadsThis tool
Catches a rewritten section or a new heading -- anything that changes the page's shape.Catches every difference between the two texts, whether or not the page's shape changed at all.
A clause added inside a paragraph that still reads naturally is easy to miss on a scan.Reports content_changed for a one-character difference exactly as reliably as for a rewritten page.
A failed page load that quietly shows a cached or stale copy can look identical to "no change".Checks fetch_status on both captures first; either one not ok reports inconclusive, never a false "unchanged".
Leaves no record beyond a person's memory of having looked.Produces a dated report -- URLs, capture timestamps, fetch status, and the verdict -- exportable as Markdown or JSON.
Free, and needs no tool beyond a browser tab.Also free, local, and needs only the two snapshots you already have.

Using both together

Nothing here argues for skipping a read of the vendor's page -- judging whether a change is friendlier or more permissive, or reading a whole new section for what it actually promises, is exactly the kind of call this tool deliberately leaves to you. The change is running the diff first, so the question stops being "did I notice anything different" and starts being "here is exactly what changed; does it matter":

Open the Vendor Change Evidence tool to diff your own snapshots, or read how do I track when a vendor changes its subprocessors or privacy policy.

Common questions

Isn't glancing at a vendor's page again good enough?

It catches a rewritten page or an obviously new section, which is real and worth doing. It is unreliable for the change that actually matters most: a few words added or removed inside a page of hundreds, in a paragraph you are not specifically looking at, worded so it reads naturally either way. A privacy page that grows from 'We process account data to provide the service' to 'We process account and usage data to provide the service' looks unchanged to someone skimming for a new heading or a bold warning, because nothing about the page's shape signals that ten words moved.

What does eyeballing two page loads actually miss, concretely?

On this tool's own shipped example, a vendor's privacy snapshot goes from 47 characters to 57 -- 'We process account data to provide the service.' becomes 'We process account and usage data to provide the service.' -- between two captures a day apart. A person opening the page twice and comparing them by eye, especially on a long real policy page rather than this one-sentence example, has to notice one clause changed inside surrounding text that reads naturally either way. Running this tool against the two snapshots reports status changed, review_required true, with the before and after lengths right there -- it does not need to notice, because it compares every character.

Can eyeballing a page ever tell you something this tool can't?

Yes -- a human reading the page can judge whether a change matters, whether new wording is friendlier or more permissive, and whether a whole new section changes what the vendor is promising. This tool deliberately does not make that judgment; its own evidence_boundary says it reports observations and the customer decides contractual or security significance. What it replaces is not judgment but noticing -- the step where a change has to be seen before anyone can judge it.

What happens when the page fails to load instead of actually being unchanged?

A person who tries to reload a vendor's page and gets a timeout, a login wall, or a CDN error page usually either notices and tries again, or -- on a routine check done quickly -- assumes the earlier capture is still good and moves on, which silently reports 'no change' when the truth is 'not checked.' This tool's compare() function checks fetch_status on both snapshots first: if either one is not ok, the result is inconclusive, not unchanged, so a failed capture can never be mistaken for a stable page.

Does this tool fetch the vendor's page for me?

No. It compares two snapshots -- url, captured_at, fetch_status, and text -- that you already have, however you captured them: a saved page, a scheduled fetch, or a copy-paste. It runs entirely in your browser and sends nothing anywhere.

← Vendor Change Evidence

Vendor Change Evidence vs. UpGuard

Different scopes: UpGuard continuously scans, scores, and questionnaires a whole portfolio of vendors for security risk. This page compares two snapshots you already captured of one vendor's policy page and reports what changed — free, local, no account.

What each tool is for

UpGuard is third-party and vendor risk management software. Its Vendor Risk product continuously scans vendors' external attack surfaces and vulnerabilities, maintains ongoing security ratings, runs security assessment questionnaires built on frameworks such as NIST, ISO, and SIG, and monitors for data exposures — reviewed and severity-rated by UpGuard's own analysts — across an organization's entire vendor portfolio, with alerting and reporting aimed at security teams and boards. It is sold as an ongoing subscription platform, and its own pricing is not something this session can verify, so no figure for it is stated here.

This tool does none of that. It does not scan a vendor's infrastructure, assign a security rating, run a questionnaire, or watch a portfolio on an ongoing basis. It takes exactly two inputs — a before and after JSON snapshot you already captured of one page (its URL, when you captured it, whether the capture succeeded, and its text) — and reports what changed between them: changed, unchanged, or inconclusive when a capture failed, never a false "unchanged". Comparison runs in your browser tab; nothing you paste is uploaded, and the tool never contacts the vendor itself. There is no account, no ongoing scan, and no per-vendor subscription.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I manage security risk across dozens or hundreds of vendors and need continuous scanning, ratings, and questionnaires.UpGuard, or a comparable vendor-risk platform — portfolio-wide continuous monitoring is not something this tool does.
I have two dated snapshots of one vendor's privacy or subprocessor page and want to know exactly what changed, right now, for free.This tool — paste both, get a source-linked diff, nothing uploaded.
I need an external security rating or attack-surface score for a vendor before we sign.UpGuard or a comparable rating service — this tool has no concept of a security score.
One snapshot capture failed or timed out — can I trust a "no changes" result?This tool reports inconclusive rather than a false "unchanged" whenever a capture's fetch_status is not ok.
Do I need to create an account, install an agent, or grant portfolio access to use it?This tool: no, ever. UpGuard is used through a subscription account across a vendor portfolio.
How do I build a habit of capturing and reviewing these snapshots myself?See how to track vendor policy changes.

Most procurement and security teams get different value from each: UpGuard (or a comparable platform) for ongoing, automated risk coverage across a whole vendor portfolio as a paid subscription, and a free tool like this one for a fast, private, source-linked answer to "what changed on this one page since the last time I looked" — useful on its own for a small team, and useful as a lightweight first check even for a team that already pays for portfolio-wide monitoring.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the comparison runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or UpGuard?

They cover different scopes. UpGuard is third-party and vendor risk management software: it continuously scans vendors' external attack surfaces, maintains security ratings, runs security assessment questionnaires (including frameworks such as NIST, ISO, and SIG), and detects data exposures across an organization's whole vendor portfolio, with alerting and board-level reporting built in. It is sold as an ongoing subscription platform aimed at security and procurement teams managing many vendor relationships at once. This tool does one narrower thing: you paste two dated snapshots you already captured of a single vendor's privacy, terms, subprocessor, or security page, and it reports what changed between them, entirely in your browser. It does not scan, score, rate, or continuously monitor anything, and it has no concept of a vendor portfolio. A team that needs ongoing, automated coverage across dozens or hundreds of vendors is the case UpGuard is built for; a team that already has two snapshots of one page and wants a fast, free, private diff and a dated record of that one review is the case this tool is built for.

Is this page affiliated with UpGuard?
